item.research_question: How can high-entropy alloying be used to stabilize locally unstable crystal phases in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) to activate their inert basal planes for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER)?
item.material_system: Pentanary TMDC high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with equimolar compositions, specifically (CrTaVHfZr)S2, (CrNbVTiZr)S2, and (MoNbTaVTi)S2, selected from a pool of group-IV (Ti, Zr, Hf), group-V (V, Nb, Ta), and group-VI (Cr, Mo, W) transition metals.
item.processing_route: Theoretical design and screening using Density Functional Theory (DFT) with the PAW method and PBE functional; structures generated as 5x5 supercells or Special Quasi-Random Structures (SQS) for pentanary alloys; stability evaluated via free energy of mixing (ΔGmix) at 1000 K and energy above convex hull (ΔHhull).
item.test_conditions: DFT calculations at T = 1000 K for thermodynamic stability; hydrogen adsorption energy (ΔGH*) calculated at standard conditions (298 K, 1 bar) on basal plane sulfur atoms; vacuum spacing of at least 20 Å; forces relaxed below 0.01 eV/Å.
key_findings: Alloying elements that prefer the 2H phase into a 1T structure (or vice versa) creates locally unstable sites that significantly enhance basal plane catalytic activity.
High-entropy alloying is essential to stabilize the target phase, as mixing entropy (ΔSmix) compensates for the positive formation enthalpy of locally unstable configurations.
Increasing the number of constituent elements from binary to pentanary enhances both thermodynamic stability and catalytic performance, with 23 stable pentanary alloys identified.
10 of the 23 predicted pentanary alloys exhibit hydrogen adsorption energies within the optimal range for HER (ΔGH* ≈ 0 eV).
Sulfur atoms surrounded by transition metals from the 'opposite' stable phase (locally unstable atoms) show the strongest hydrogen binding due to p-band centers closer to the Fermi level.
Predicted pentanary HEAs show higher stability and catalytic activity compared to the experimentally synthesized (CrMoWReMn)S2.
Sulfur atoms are consistently more active than neighboring metal atoms for hydrogen adsorption across unary, binary, and HEA systems.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that catalytic activity correlates with local structural instability; by alloying elements that prefer one phase into a structure dominated by elements preferring the opposite phase, 'locally unstable' sites are created. These sites possess a higher density of states with pz character near the Fermi level, leading to stronger hydrogen adsorption. The global stability of the alloy is maintained by the high configurational entropy of the high-entropy mixture, which stabilizes the otherwise metastable phase.
item.limitations: The study was limited to low hydrogen coverage regimes where adsorbate-adsorbate interactions are negligible; the analysis focused on equimolar compositions, excluding nonequimolar variations; the p-band center descriptor is less reliable for complex HEA structures compared to unary/binary systems; and the SQS models may not capture all rare adsorption environments in 2H-phase alloys.
item.future_work: The authors propose combining computational approaches with machine learning to accelerate the exploration of nonequimolar HEA compositions and to predict configurational entropy; they suggest investigating hydrogen-hydrogen repulsion effects at high coverage regimes; and they emphasize the critical need for experimental validation of the predicted stable and active HEAs.
quotes: high densities of catalytically active sites can be formed on the TMDC basal plane by alloying elements that prefer the 2H (1T) phase into a 1T (2H) structure.
mixing entropy plays a decisive role in stabilizing the alloy, implying that high-entropy alloying becomes essential.
by alloying locally unstable elements into a globally stable structure, it is possible to combine good overall stability with high local reactivity.
